plate_findings.evidence: Initial erythematous nodule on right-hand finger day 1 following goat bite
Lesion with central yellow-brown crust on day 59

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: Clinical photograph of day 1 orf lesion presenting as an erythematous finger nodule consistent with classic early orf presentation. B: Clinical photograph of day 15 orf lesion showing a targetoid whitish nodule with surrounding erythema, consistent with classic orf evolution. C: Clinical photograph of day 29 orf lesion showing a developing targetoid nodule with discoloration and capsule formation, consistent with classic orf progression. D: Clinical photograph of day 59 orf lesion showing a central umbilicated crust, a classic feature of mature orf lesions. E: Clinical photograph of day 78 orf lesion in the healing stage, showing a faint circular residual mark consistent with resolving orf. F: Clinical photograph of day 87 orf lesion in late healing stage, showing near-complete resolution with a faint residual mark.
panels.attribution_text: Sobral et al. Genomic characterization of the first goat-associated orf virus genome sequenced directly from a human clinical sample in Portugal.. Archives of virology 2026. doi:10.1007/s00705-026-06749-4. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Temporal evolution of a finger lesion following a goat bite. (A) Day 1. Initial lesion on the finger immediately after a goat bite. (B) Day 15. After careful wound cleaning and disinfection, a small whitish nodule surrounded by an erythematous halo appeared. The lesion was punctured due to suspicion of purulent content; however, no material was expressed. (C, D) Days 29–59. The lesion became reddish with dark red and black spots, developing a firm capsule-like structure. It remained sensitive and painful on pressure. A biopsy was performed on day 44, and sutures were removed on day 57. (E, F) Day > 78. Healing stage. The skin remained slightly sensitive and not fully smooth, with a faint circular mark at the site of the previous lesion
in_text_mentions: A cutaneous biopsy was obtained from a 23-year-old female veterinary medicine student presenting with a 5 mm solitary erythematous nodule on her right-hand finger (Fig. 1), approximately four weeks after being bitten by a goat reported to have visible oral lesions (though specific diagnosis of the animal was not performed). The initial histopathological examination suggested chondroma, inconsistent with the clinical presentation and epidemiological history, prompting molecular investigation at INSA. DNA was extracted using the QIAamp DNA Mini Kit (Qiagen). Parapoxvirus detection was performed

plate_findings.evidence: Targetoid nodule with a necrotic center, a white ring, and peripheral erythema on the right little finger

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Clinical photograph of a 30-year-old human orf patient showing the characteristic targetoid finger nodule with necrotic center, white ring, and peripheral erythema as described in the figure caption. B: Hematoxylin and eosin stained histologic section (50× magnification) from the same orf patient showing marked epidermal acanthosis and hyperkeratosis, consistent with orf infection as described in the caption. C: Higher magnification hematoxylin and eosin stained histologic section (400× magnification) from the same orf patient demonstrating dermal vascular proliferation and granulocytic/eosinophilic inflammatory infiltration as described in the figure caption.
panels.attribution_text: Coradduzza et al. Molecular Insights into the Genetic Variability of ORF Virus in a Mediterranean Region (Sardinia, Italy).. Life (Basel, Switzerland) 2021. doi:10.3390/life11050416. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Nodule on the right little finger of a 30-year-old sheep farmer infected with ORFV. (A) Targetoid nodule with a necrotic center, a white ring, and peripheral erythema. (B) Microscopical appearance of the skin of the ORF-infected man, characterized by marked acanthosis and hyperkeratosis. Hematoxylin and eosin staining (H&E). Original magnification 50×. Scale bar = 250 µm. (C) In the dermis, vascular proliferation with granulocytic and eosinophilic infiltration. Hematoxylin and eosin staining (H&E). Original magnification 400×. Scale bar = 100 µm.
in_text_mentions: In the 30-year-old sheep farmer who was brought to our attention, a red plaque on a finger was observed. The lesion evolved into a targetoid nodule with a necrotic center, a white ring, and peripheral erythema (Figure 3A). The nodule was subsequently followed by a dry crust and resolved without scarring.

re 2C). The severe manifestation of ORFV infection was histologically characterized by massive proliferative patterns involving the epithelium and the fibrovascular component of the lamina propria of the mucosae as well as of the dermis of the skin (Figure 2D). Marked acanthosis, hyperkeratosis with parakeratotic crusts, and edema of the superficial dermis were histopathologically observed in the human lesion (Figure 3B). In addition, the dermis exhibited vascular proliferation together with granulocytic and eosinophilic infiltration, showing a tendency towards abscessualization (Figure 3B,C).

plate_findings.evidence: ulcerated violaceous nodule; central necrotic area

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Clinical photograph of human patients (63-year-old female and her daughter) showing erythematous-violaceous papules and ulcerated violaceous nodules on fingers, consistent with classic orf presentation. B: Clinical photograph showing a violaceous erythematous targetoid lesion with central umbilicated crust on the thumb, consistent with orf infection in the patient's daughter.
panels.attribution_text: Rezende et al. Clinical Manifestation, Dermoscopy, and Scanning Electron Microscopy in Two Cases of Contagious Ecthyma (Orf Nodule).. Case reports in dermatological medicine 2018. doi:10.1155/2018/2094086. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: (a) Erythematous-violaceous papules and an ulcerated violaceous nodule on the patient's (left) and her daughter's (right) fingers; (b) a violaceous erythematous lesion with red outer ring, and erythematous border on the right thumb of patient's daughter.
in_text_mentions: A 63-year-old female came for consultation presenting with an erythematous violaceous plaque on the right index finger that had started 7 days previously. On examination a central necrotic area (Figure 1(a)) was observed. Fracture and acute vascular occlusion were excluded. Laboratory tests were unremarkable. A consultation with the dermatology department was then requested.

while performing this task. During the evaluation of the patient, it was observed that the patient's daughter presented with a similar skin lesion on the left thumb, and she reported that she also helped to feed the little goats. Dermatology exam showed an indurated nodule with central umbilication covered by crust and surrounded by a reddish halo (Figure 1(b)). Dermoscopy of the finger nodule showed an erythematous area, central ulceration, yellow crust, brown dots, a white structureless area partially surrounding the lesion, and dotted vessels (Figure 2). The diagnosis of orf was suspected.

On the basis of clinical suspicion of ecthyma contagiosum, we obtained a cutaneous biopsy specimen for biologic confirmations by PCR and histologic analysis. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (a, b, c, d). a: Clinical photograph of the scalp showing an erythematous, weeping, infiltrated noduloplaque with cobblestone appearance, consistent with Orf infection occurring at an unusual scalp location. b: Close-up clinical photograph demonstrating the size (4×4 cm) and weeping nature of the scalp noduloplaque characteristic of Orf. c: Low-power histology showing epidermal acanthosis with finger-like downward projections and dermal inflammatory infiltrate, consistent with the histologic changes seen in Orf. d: High-power histology demonstrating intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions in vacuolated epidermal cells, a characteristic histopathologic feature of Orf caused by parapoxvirus.

panels.figure_caption: (A) Lesion on acute stage. A 3 cm well-defined, erythematous, edematous, centrally ulcerated, hemorrhagic moderately hard, and fragile nodule at the left eyebrow tip, (B) Lesion on regenerative stage. A 3.5 cm hemorrhagic crusted nodule after cauterization, (C) Lesion on papillomatous stage. A 3 cm erythematous and fragile nodule with papillomatous projections, (D) Lesion on regression stage. A 2 cm skin-colored plaque with mild and superficially papillomatous projections, (E) Healed lesion.
in_text_mentions: A 54-year-old otherwise healthy man presented with a bleeding mass at his left eyebrow tip for 2 weeks in the dermatology outpatient clinic. He had a history of suturing after traumatic erosion by a sheep 1 week before the appearance of the lesion at the feast of sacrifice. Dermatologic examination revealed a 3 cm well-defined, erythematous, edematous, centrally ulcerated, hemorrhagic, moderately hard, and fragile nodule at the left eyebrow tip (Fig. 1A).

. He was diagnosed with pyogenic granuloma, and therefore treated with cauterization superficially. Due to the persisted lesion, he reapplied to our dermatology outpatient clinic and he was advised to avoid any surgical intervention because of the aggravation. He was followed up with wet dressing and fusidic acid ointment. The photographs of patients were recorded at the follow-up visits (Fig. 1B–E). The patient was continued to be followed up without any intervention because of regression of the lesion at the follow-up visits. The lesion resolved spontaneously in 6 weeks without any scarring.

The lesion evolves through six clinical stages: Maculopapular stage, targetoid stage, acute stage (weeping nodule), regenerative dry stage with black dots, papillomatous stage, and regression stage with a dry crust [2]. In our case, disease was on the acute stage during application to our clinic (Fig. 1A). Papillomatous and regression stages were observed and showed in Figure 1C and d; but regenerative stage was not typical with black dots because of cauterization of the lesion (Fig. 1B).
